consensus_summary: Consensus primarily identifies the term with the four living creatures of the Ezekiel and Revelation throne visions: exalted cherubim-class angelic attendants who surround God’s throne, proclaim holiness, and most commonly symbolize the whole of animate creation (lion/ox/man/eagle faces); major alternatives include the four Evangelists and attributes of Christ. A separate non-symbolic lexical sense denotes ordinary animate beings (as in Genesis).
book_summary: The book identifies living creatures (those in Revelation’s sea) as peoples/nations, by direct analogy to the beasts that rise from Daniel’s sea and represent kingdoms.
consensus_core_identification: four cherubim/throne attendants symbolizing animate creation (or Evangelists)
boundary_disagreement: None applicable; book’s referent (sea creatures as peoples) lies outside the consensus scope of throne attendants and ordinary animals.
material_contradiction: None; the identification is simply unattested in the consensus rather than contradicted by it.
rationale: Reducing both to minimal cores shows the consensus locked on the throne-vision zōa (cherubim representing creation or Evangelists) plus a lexical sense of animate beings, none of which equates living creatures with nations/peoples. The book’s parallel (Daniel sea-beasts = kingdoms 	o Revelation sea living-creatures = peoples) is absent from every primary meaning and listed alternative, satisfying the definition of novelty as absence of coverage rather than contradiction or boundary refinement of a shared referent.
strongest_objection: The cited Revelation verses use ordinary language for sea animals dying in the plagues (different Greek terms from the throne zōa) and supply no symbolic equation to peoples; the Daniel parallel governs beasts/kingdoms only.
